issues.summary: Epic 1 — Team and User Administration
issues.description:
Phase 1 — Core Task Management

Goal

As a Super Admin, I need to create teams, add employees, and assign team leads so that the company structure can be represented in the system.

This epic establishes the foundation everything else stands on: the project skeleton, the identity model, and the authorisation rules that every later endpoint will depend on.

Architecture baseline (applies to all epics)

Modular monolith using a layered design pattern. Every module follows the same shape:

module/
├── controller   — HTTP boundary: routing, request/response, Zod validation
├── service      — business logic, authorisation rules, orchestration
├── repository   — data access, TypeORM queries
└── entity       — TypeORM entity definitions

Rules: controllers never touch repositories directly; business rules live in services, not controllers; cross-module reads go through the other module's service, not its repository.

ORM: TypeORM (decided — not Prisma).

In scope

Backend

- Express + TypeScript project setup, PostgreSQL, TypeORM, migrations
- Layered folder structure established for the auth, users, and teams modules — this epic sets the pattern the rest of the build copies
- User, Team, TeamMember entities
- Role enum: SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD, EMPLOYEE
- Endpoints: create user, create team, add member to team, assign team lead
- Login + JWT authentication
- Role-based authorization middleware
- Seed data for users and teams

Frontend

- React application scaffold
- Login screen
- Role-based navigation
- Teams page, Team Details page
- User creation form, Team creation form
- Employee assignment and team-lead assignment interfaces

Out of scope

- Goals, tasks, and assignments (Epic 2)
- Any time recording (Epic 3)
- Dashboards or reporting (Epic 4)
- Password reset, email verification, SSO, multi-tenancy
- User profile pages and avatars (optional polish, Epic 6)

Acceptance criteria

- Super Admin can log in
- Super Admin can create a team
- Super Admin can create users
- Super Admin can add members to a team
- Exactly one team lead can be assigned to a team
- Employees cannot access administration endpoints (403, verified by test)
- Each module is split into controller / service / repository / entity layers

Dependencies

- Blocks: Epic 2, Epic 3, Epic 4, Epic 5, Epic 6 — every downstream epic requires the user/team model and the auth middleware
- Depends on: nothing; this is the entry point of the build
- Key risk: the role-based authorization middleware is reused everywhere. Get its contract right here rather than retrofitting it later.
- Open decision: the doc says User belongs to Team (singular) but also defines a team_members join table. Settle whether a person can belong to more than one team before writing the first migration — the allocation maths in Epic 4 depends on the answer.

issues.summary: Epic 2 — Goal, Task, and Assignment Management
issues.description:
Phase 1 — Core Task Management

Goal

As a Team Lead, I need to create team goals, break them into tasks, and assign employees so that the team can complete work before the deadline.

This epic delivers the core domain of the product: the Goal → Task → Assignee chain that every later feature reads from.

Domain structure

Team Goal
├── Goal title
├── Description
├── Start date
├── Deadline
├── Status
└── Tasks
    ├── Assignee
    ├── Priority
    ├── Status
    └── Estimated hours

In scope

Backend

- Goal, Task models; TaskAssignment if multiple assignees are allowed
- Goal statuses: PLANNED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED
- Task statuses: TODO, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, DONE
- Priorities: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH
- Endpoints: create goal, create task, assign task, update task status, list team goals, list employee tasks
- Authorization rules: Team Leads manage only their own team; employees update only their assigned tasks

Frontend

- Team Goals page, Goal Details page
- Goal form, Task form, task-assignment control
- Employee "My Tasks" page with status update control
- Display deadline, priority, assignee, status
- Simple progress percentage per goal

Out of scope

- Time recording against tasks (Epic 3)
- Cross-team or company-wide rollups (Epic 4)
- Task dependencies and calculated priority scores (Epic 5) — this epic uses the manual priority field only
- Comments, attachments, drag-and-drop boards

Acceptance criteria

- Team Lead can create a goal for their team
- Team Lead can add tasks under the goal
- Team Lead can assign a team member
- Employee sees only assigned tasks
- Employee can change an assigned task's status
- Goal progress is calculated from completed tasks

Dependencies

- Depends on: Epic 1 (users, teams, roles, auth middleware)
- Blocks: Epic 3 (timesheets attach to tasks), Epic 4 (allocation reads estimated hours and task counts), Epic 5 (dependencies and scoring extend Task), Epic 6 (risk detection reads deadlines and statuses)
- Design note: estimated_hours on Task is set here but only becomes meaningful in Epic 4. Include the field now to avoid a migration later.

issues.summary: Epic 3 — Employee Timesheets
issues.description:
Phase 2 — Timesheets and Resource Management

Goal

As an employee, I need to record time spent on an assigned task for each day so that my team lead can understand effort and progress.

This epic turns the system from a task list into an effort-tracking tool. The estimated-vs-actual comparison it produces is the raw material for every dashboard in Epic 4.

Timesheet entry fields

Employee
Task
Work date
Hours spent
Work description
Submission status
Created time
Updated time

In scope

Backend

- TimesheetEntry model with work date, hours spent, employee work note
- Validation: maximum daily hours, no negative time
- Prevent logging time against unassigned tasks
- Prevent duplicate entries for the same task and date, or update the existing entry instead
- Endpoints: create, update, delete own entry, employee timesheet history, task total hours
- Calculate actual hours against estimated hours

Frontend

- "Log Time" action on assigned tasks
- Daily timesheet form
- "My Timesheet" page with date filtering
- Totals by day and by task
- Estimated versus actual hours display
- Input validation and error messages

Out of scope

- Approval or submission workflow beyond a simple status field
- Team-level and company-level aggregation views (Epic 4)
- CSV export (optional polish, Epic 6)
- Billing, invoicing, payroll, or cost rates
- Automatic time tracking, timers, or idle detection

Acceptance criteria

- Employee can log time only for an assigned task
- Employee can update their own time entry
- Team Lead can view time recorded against team tasks
- Task details show total recorded time
- Invalid hour values are rejected

Dependencies

- Depends on: Epic 1 (employee identity), Epic 2 (Task and assignment must exist before time can attach to them)
- Blocks: Epic 4 — recorded hours are one half of the workload calculation; Epic 6 — the "actual hours exceed estimate" risk condition reads from this data
- Decision to settle early: the duplicate-entry rule. Reject the second entry, or upsert into the first? Both are defensible; pick one before writing the endpoint, because the frontend form behaviour follows from it.

issues.summary: Epic 4 — Resource Allocation and Team Overview
issues.description:
Phase 2 — Timesheets and Resource Management

Goal

As a manager or Team Lead, I need to see how work is distributed among employees so that I can identify overloaded and underutilised resources.

This epic answers the questions from the problem statement that no single screen could answer before: who is overloaded, who is available, and is the goal on track.

In scope

Backend

- Team-allocation summary endpoint
- Per-employee calculations: active tasks, estimated assigned hours, actual recorded hours, completed-task count, overdue-task count
- Team-goal progress calculation
- Date-range filters; project or goal filters
- Company-wide summary endpoint for Super Admin

Frontend

- Team Dashboard: active goals, total / completed / blocked / overdue tasks
- Employee workload table showing assigned hours versus recorded hours
- Super Admin company overview
- Filters for team, employee, and date range

Workload rule

0–60% capacity   = Available
61–90% capacity  = Balanced
Above 90%        = Overloaded

Weekly capacity is configurable; use 40 hours as the simulation default.

Out of scope

- Priority scoring and recommendations (Epic 5)
- Risk detection and alerting (Epic 6) — this epic displays overdue counts, it does not flag them as risks
- Forecasting, capacity planning across future weeks, or scenario modelling
- Per-person cost or billing rates

Acceptance criteria

- Team Lead can see resource allocation for their own team
- Super Admin can see all teams
- Dashboard shows overloaded and available employees
- Estimated and actual effort are both visible
- Employees cannot view other employees' timesheets

Dependencies

- Depends on: Epic 2 (estimated hours, task counts, goal deadlines), Epic 3 (recorded hours — without it the workload column is half empty)
- Blocks: Epic 6 — the "employee overloaded" risk condition reuses this capacity calculation, so expose it as a service rather than inlining it in the endpoint
- Watch for: aggregation queries here will be the first place performance shows. Consider whether totals are computed on read or maintained incrementally.

issues.summary: Epic 5 — Task Prioritization and Work Recommendations
issues.description:
Phase 3 — Prioritization, Risk, and Advanced Features

Goal

As a Team Lead, I need the system to rank tasks so that the team works on the most important available work first.

This is where the application stops being a record of work and starts making a recommendation. The scoring must be explainable — a ranking nobody understands is a ranking nobody trusts.

Priority signals

Manual business priority · deadline urgency · number of dependent tasks · task status · blocked state · estimated effort · goal importance

Scoring model

Priority score =
  Business priority
+ Deadline urgency
+ Dependency impact
+ Goal importance
- Blocked penalty

High priority:       +30      Due within 2 days:   +30
Medium priority:     +20      Due within 7 days:   +20
Low priority:        +10      Due later:            +5

Blocks another task: +10 per task
Currently blocked:   -40

In scope

Backend

- TaskDependency model; task-priority score and business-impact level fields
- Prevent direct self-dependency; detect basic circular dependencies
- Calculate blocked-task state and priority score
- Recommended-tasks endpoint with a per-task explanation
- Recalculate ranking when deadlines, status, or dependencies change

Frontend

- Dependency selector on the task form
- Display blocked-by / blocks relationships
- Recommended Tasks section with priority score and reasons
- Sorting by calculated priority; highlight high-impact tasks

Out of scope

- Machine learning, historical-outcome learning, or adaptive weights — the weights are fixed constants
- Automatic assignment or scheduling; the system recommends, a human decides
- Multi-level critical-path analysis or Gantt scheduling
- Risk detection and alerts (Epic 6)

Acceptance criteria

- Tasks can depend on other tasks
- Circular dependencies are rejected
- Blocked tasks are identified
- Available tasks are ranked
- Team Lead can understand why a task received its score

Dependencies

- Depends on: Epic 2 (Task, priority, deadline, status), Epic 4 (assignee availability feeds the "assigned employee is available" reason)
- Blocks: Epic 6 — the "high-priority task blocked" risk condition reads the blocked state computed here
- Hardest part: cycle detection. A depth-limited DFS over the dependency edges on write is enough for this scale; decide whether the check runs on every write or only on dependency creation.

issues.summary: Epic 6 — Risk Dashboard, Notifications, and Audit History
issues.description:
Phase 3 — Prioritization, Risk, and Advanced Features

Goal

As a manager, I need the system to highlight delivery risks and important changes so that I can act before deadlines are missed.

This epic is the largest of the six and covers four related concerns: risk detection, activity logging, notifications, and search/filtering. Treat them as separable if Day 3 runs short — risk detection is the one that must ship.

Risk conditions

Goal deadline approaching · goal progress below expectation · high-priority task blocked · task overdue · unassigned task · employee overloaded · actual hours exceed estimate · task has no recent progress

In scope

Backend

- Project-risk calculation service covering all eight conditions above
- ActivityLog model; log task status changes, assignments, priority changes, timesheet updates
- Recent-activity endpoint
- Basic in-app notifications
- Search and filtering endpoints

Frontend

- Risk Overview section with Low / Medium / High severity
- Overdue-task cards, blocked-task cards, overloaded-resource warnings
- Recent-activity timeline
- Global task search; filters by team, status, assignee, deadline, priority
- Simple charts for goal progress and resource allocation
- Improved loading, empty, and error states

Optional polish (only after the main workflow works)

Dark mode · drag-and-drop task board · CSV timesheet export · goal progress chart · employee utilisation chart · deadline notifications · task comments · avatar and profile pages · dashboard date-range filters

Out of scope

- Email, Slack, or push notification delivery — in-app only
- Predictive or ML-based risk scoring; the conditions are deterministic rules
- Full audit trail with field-level diffs and rollback
- Full-text search infrastructure; database filtering is sufficient at this scale

Acceptance criteria

- Managers can see project risks in one place
- Overdue and blocked work is clearly visible
- Important actions appear in the audit history
- Tasks can be searched and filtered
- Super Admin sees company-wide information
- Team Leads see only their team's information

Dependencies

- Depends on: Epic 2 (deadlines, statuses), Epic 3 (estimate overruns), Epic 4 (overload calculation), Epic 5 (blocked state) — this epic consumes all four and should reuse their services rather than re-deriving the logic
- Blocks: nothing; this is the final epic
- Scope-cut order if Day 3 compresses: drop optional polish first, then search/filtering, then notifications, then activity logging. Risk detection is the deliverable that makes Phase 3 meaningful.

issues.summary: Backend scaffold: Express, TypeORM, PostgreSQL, and the layered module structure
issues.description:
Story

As a developer, I need a running backend skeleton with the layered structure in place so that every subsequent story has an obvious home for its code.

This is the only horizontal story in the backlog. It exists because the layering convention must be demonstrated once before it can be copied.

Layer work

Entity — TypeORM DataSource configured against PostgreSQL; migration tooling wired and a first empty migration proven to run and roll back.

Repository — a thin BaseRepository wrapper if useful, so modules aren't each inventing their own query conventions.

Service — no domain logic yet; establish the pattern that services receive repositories by constructor injection.

Controller — health-check endpoint at GET /health returning DB connectivity, proving the full stack from route to database.

Also in scope

- Express + TypeScript project, tsconfig, linting, hot reload
- Docker Compose: api and postgres services, one-command startup
- Zod set up as the validation layer at the controller boundary
- Centralised error handler translating thrown domain errors into HTTP status codes
- Module folders created empty and committed: auth, users, teams, goals, tasks, timesheets, dashboards, audit
- .env handling and config module

Target structure

src/
├── modules/
│   └── <module>/
│       ├── <module>.controller.ts
│       ├── <module>.service.ts
│       ├── <module>.repository.ts
│       └── <module>.entity.ts
├── common/
│   ├── errors/
│   ├── middleware/
│   └── config/
└── data-source.ts

Acceptance criteria

- docker compose up starts API and database with no manual steps
- GET /health returns 200 and confirms a live database connection
- A migration can be generated, applied, and reverted
- The four-layer folder convention exists and is documented in the README
- Invalid request bodies are rejected by Zod with a consistent error shape

Notes

The centralised error handler is worth doing now rather than later. Without it, every controller invents its own try/catch and the authorisation failures in the next story become inconsistent.

issues.summary: User login with JWT authentication
issues.description:
Story

As any user, I need to log in with my email and password and receive a token so that the system knows who I am on every subsequent request.

Layer work

Entity — User (id, email unique, passwordHash, name, role, createdAt, updatedAt). Role enum: SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD, EMPLOYEE. The plaintext password is never a column.

Repository — UserRepository.findByEmail(email).

Service — AuthService.login(email, password): look up user, compare hash with bcrypt, sign a JWT carrying userId and role, return token plus a safe user projection. Throws a single generic InvalidCredentialsError whether the email is unknown or the password is wrong.

Controller — POST /auth/login, Zod-validated body. GET /auth/me returning the current user from the token.

Frontend

- Login screen with email/password and inline error display
- Token stored and attached to all API calls via an axios/fetch interceptor
- Auth context holding the current user and role
- Protected route wrapper redirecting unauthenticated users to login
- Role-based navigation: Super Admin, Team Lead, and Employee each see a different menu
- Logout clearing the token and redirecting

Acceptance criteria

- A seeded user can log in and receive a valid JWT
- Wrong password and unknown email produce the same error message and status
- Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes; no endpoint ever returns passwordHash
- GET /auth/me returns the caller's identity and role
- An expired or malformed token is rejected with 401
- The navigation menu differs by role after login

Decisions to settle here

- Token lifetime. Pick a fixed expiry (24h is fine for a simulation) and skip refresh tokens — they are explicitly out of scope, but the expiry needs a number.
- Token storage on the client. localStorage is simplest; note the trade-off rather than pretending it's ideal.

Dependencies

Depends on the backend scaffold. Blocks every other story in the project — nothing can be authorised until identity exists.

issues.summary: Role-based authorization middleware and scope enforcement
issues.description:
Story

As the system, I need to reject requests from users who lack the required role or team scope so that data stays confined to the people entitled to see it.

This is the single most reused piece of code in the application. Six epics assume it works.

Layer work

Common middleware — requireAuth verifies the JWT and attaches req.user ({ userId, role }). requireRole(...roles) rejects with 403 when the role doesn't match.

Service — scope checks belong here, not in middleware, because they need data. Establish the convention now:

- assertTeamLeadOf(userId, teamId) — throws unless the caller leads that team
- assertMemberOf(userId, teamId) — throws unless the caller belongs to that team
- assertOwnsResource(userId, resourceOwnerId) — throws unless the caller owns the record

Controller — routes declare their role requirement declaratively; controllers never contain if (user.role === ...) branches.

Error contract

- No token, expired token, malformed token → 401
- Valid token, insufficient role or scope → 403
- Resource exists but is outside the caller's scope → 403, not 404

Acceptance criteria

- An Employee calling any Super Admin endpoint receives 403
- A Team Lead calling another team's endpoints receives 403
- An unauthenticated request to any protected route receives 401
- Role checks are declared at the route, and scope checks live in services
- Tests cover at least one positive and one negative case per role

Notes

Why 403 and not 404 for out-of-scope resources. Returning 404 hides whether the record exists, which is stricter. Returning 403 is simpler and easier to debug in a simulation. Either is defensible — but pick one and apply it everywhere, because inconsistency here is the kind of thing that looks like a bug for the rest of the build.

The rule that keeps this maintainable: authorisation lives in exactly two places — role at the route, scope in the service. The moment a controller starts inspecting req.user.role, the pattern has broken.

Dependencies

Depends on JWT authentication. Blocks all of Epics 2–6.

issues.summary: Super Admin creates and lists user accounts
issues.description:
Story

As a Super Admin, I need to create user accounts with a name, email and role so that employees and team leads exist in the system before teams are formed.

Layer work

Entity — User, already defined in the login story. This story adds nothing to the schema.

Repository — create, findById, findAll(filter), existsByEmail.

Service — UserService.createUser(dto): reject duplicate emails with a domain error, hash the supplied password, persist, return a projection without the hash. UserService.listUsers(filter) supports filtering by role and by unassigned status, which the team-assignment screen needs.

Controller — POST /users and GET /users, both Super Admin only. Zod schema enforces a valid email, a minimum password length, and a role drawn from the enum.

Frontend

- Users list page with role filter
- User creation form: name, email, password, role selector
- Duplicate-email error surfaced against the email field, not as a generic banner
- Success feedback and list refresh after creation

Acceptance criteria

- Super Admin can create a user with any of the three roles
- A duplicate email is rejected with a clear message and no partial record is written
- Team Lead and Employee both receive 403 on POST /users and GET /users
- The response never contains passwordHash
- The users list can be filtered to those not yet assigned to a team

Notes

The "unassigned users" filter looks like a nice-to-have but the team-membership story depends on it — without it, the assignment screen has no sensible list to offer.

Password handling here is deliberately crude: the Super Admin sets an initial password directly. Invitation emails and forced password change are out of scope for the simulation.

Dependencies

Depends on the authorization middleware. Blocks team membership assignment and the seed dataset.

issues.summary: Super Admin creates teams and views team details
issues.description:
Story

As a Super Admin, I need to create teams and view a team's details so that the company structure is represented before goals and tasks are created against it.

Layer work

Entity — Team (id, name unique, description, teamLeadId nullable FK to User, weeklyCapacityHours default 40, createdAt, updatedAt).

Repository — create, findById, findAll, findByIdWithMembers, existsByName.

Service — TeamService.createTeam(dto) rejecting duplicate names. TeamService.getTeamDetails(teamId, caller) returning the team with its lead and members, scoped: Super Admin sees any team, a Team Lead sees only their own, an Employee sees only teams they belong to.

Controller — POST /teams (Super Admin), GET /teams (scoped by role), GET /teams/:id (scoped).

Frontend

- Teams list page — all teams for Super Admin, own team for a Team Lead
- Team creation form: name, description, weekly capacity
- Team Details page showing the lead, the member list, and member count
- Empty state when a team has no members yet

Acceptance criteria

- Super Admin can create a team with a unique name
- A duplicate team name is rejected
- Super Admin sees all teams; a Team Lead sees only the team they lead
- Team Details shows the current lead and all members
- A team can be created with no lead and no members, and the UI handles that state
- Employees receive 403 on POST /teams

Notes

weeklyCapacityHours lives on the team. The three-day doc says capacity should be configurable and suggests 40 hours. Putting it on Team rather than hard-coding a constant costs nothing now and is what makes the Epic 4 workload bands meaningful. If it later needs to vary per person, it moves to User — but team-level is the right default.

A team is created with a null lead because the lead must already exist as a user, and ordering the two operations the other way round creates a chicken-and-egg problem in the UI.

Dependencies

Depends on user creation. Blocks team membership, and all of Epic 2 — goals belong to teams.

issues.summary: Assign employees to a team and designate a team lead
issues.description:
Story

As a Super Admin, I need to add employees to a team and designate one of them as the team lead so that work can be assigned and supervised within a defined group.

Layer work

Entity — TeamMember join table (id, teamId, userId, joinedAt) with a unique constraint on (teamId, userId). Team.teamLeadId is set by this story's lead-assignment path.

Repository — addMember, removeMember, findMembersByTeam, findTeamsByUser, isMember.

Service

- TeamService.addMember(teamId, userId) — rejects if the user is already a member; enforces the membership rule decided below
- TeamService.assignTeamLead(teamId, userId) — the user must already be a member of the team; promotes their role to TEAM_LEAD; demotes the previous lead to EMPLOYEE; enforces exactly one lead per team
- TeamService.removeMember(teamId, userId) — rejects removing the current lead without first reassigning

Controller — POST /teams/:id/members, DELETE /teams/:id/members/:userId, PUT /teams/:id/lead. All Super Admin only.

Frontend

- Employee assignment interface on Team Details: pick from unassigned users, add to team
- Team lead selector, restricted to current members of that team
- Confirmation when replacing an existing lead, showing who is being demoted
- Remove-member action with the "reassign the lead first" error surfaced clearly

Acceptance criteria

- Super Admin can add one or more employees to a team
- Exactly one team lead exists per team; assigning a new one demotes the previous
- A user who is not a member of the team cannot be made its lead
- Adding the same user twice is rejected
- Removing the current lead is blocked until a replacement is assigned
- A Team Lead cannot add members to a team they do not lead

Blocking decision — settle before writing the migration

The source doc contradicts itself: the relationship diagram says User belongs to Team (one team), but a team_members join table implies many. Pick one:

- One team per user — add a unique constraint on TeamMember.userId. Simpler, and makes the Epic 4 workload maths unambiguous: a person's capacity belongs to exactly one team.
- Many teams per user — no such constraint. More realistic, but then weekly capacity is shared across teams and every allocation figure needs a rule for splitting it.

Recommendation: one team per user for the simulation. The realism gained isn't worth the ambiguity it introduces into every dashboard downstream. Record whichever you choose as an ADR — it is exactly the kind of decision the context engine should later surface.

Dependencies

Depends on user creation and team creation. Blocks Epic 2 (task assignment validates team membership) and Epic 4 (allocation groups by team).

issues.summary: Seed demo dataset: users, teams, memberships, and leads
issues.description:
Story

As a developer, I need a repeatable seed script that populates a realistic company structure so that every later feature can be developed and demonstrated against consistent data.

Layer work

Seed script — npm run seed, idempotent: running it twice must not duplicate records. It calls services, not repositories, so the seeded data obeys the same validation rules real data does.

Dataset (per the source doc)

1  Super Admin
2  Team Leads
6  Employees
2  Teams          — Platform Team, Frontend Team

Later stories extend the same script with goals, tasks, timesheets, and dependencies. Structure it so each epic appends its own seed module rather than rewriting one large file.

Acceptance criteria

- npm run seed populates users, teams, memberships, and leads in one command
- Running it a second time leaves the database unchanged
- Every seeded user can log in with a documented password
- Both teams have a lead and at least three members
- Seeded credentials are listed in the README

Why this story matters more than it looks

TrackIt exists to generate input for the Context Core engine, and that engine's value depends on cross-reference density — artifacts that point at each other. A repository of random data produces a generic retrieval demo; a dataset where the same people, teams and identifiers recur across tickets, code and commits is what makes context compilation demonstrable.

So seed with intent:

- Use stable, named identities that will reappear in commit messages, PR descriptions and ticket comments. Alex, Priya and Sam are already named in the source doc's allocation example — reuse them rather than inventing new names.
- Keep the team names from the doc (Platform Team, Frontend Team) so they match the goal names seeded in Epic 2.
- Make the two teams structurally different — one larger and one smaller — so allocation dashboards have something to contrast.

Dependencies

Depends on user creation, team creation, and membership assignment. Blocks nothing directly, but every later demo and every subsequent seed module builds on it.

issues.summary: Team Lead creates and manages team goals
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need to create a goal for my team with a start date and deadline so that a body of work has an owner, a shape and a due date.

Layer work

Entity — Goal (id, teamId FK, title, description, startDate, deadline, status, importance, createdById, createdAt, updatedAt). Status enum: PLANNED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED.

Repository — create, findById, findByTeam(teamId, filter), update.

Service — GoalService.createGoal(dto, caller): calls assertTeamLeadOf(caller, teamId), validates that the deadline falls after the start date, defaults status to PLANNED. GoalService.listTeamGoals(teamId, caller) scoped so a Team Lead sees their team's goals, an Employee sees goals of the team they belong to, and a Super Admin sees any.

Controller — POST /goals, GET /teams/:teamId/goals, GET /goals/:id, PATCH /goals/:id.

Frontend

- Team Goals page listing goals with title, deadline, status and progress
- Goal creation form: title, description, start date, deadline, importance
- Goal Details page — the shell that the tasks story fills in
- Status badge and a visual marker for goals past their deadline
- Empty state when a team has no goals

Acceptance criteria

- A Team Lead can create a goal for their own team
- A Team Lead creating a goal for another team receives 403
- A deadline before the start date is rejected
- Goals are listed with status and deadline visible
- An Employee can view their team's goals but cannot create one
- Super Admin can view goals across all teams

Notes

importance is added here but consumed in Epic 5. The priority-scoring formula includes "goal importance" as a signal, so the field needs to exist before scoring is built. Add it now to avoid a second migration. A simple three-level enum matching the task priority levels is enough.

On status. Keep it manually set for now. It is tempting to derive COMPLETED automatically once all tasks are done, but that conflicts with CANCELLED being a deliberate human act — and progress percentage already communicates completion. Leave derivation out.

Dependencies

Depends on team creation and the authorization middleware. Blocks task creation and goal progress.

issues.summary: Team Lead creates tasks under a goal
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need to break a goal into individual tasks with priorities, deadlines and effort estimates so that the work becomes assignable units.

Layer work

Entity — Task (id, goalId FK, title, description, status, priority, estimatedHours, dueDate, assigneeId nullable FK, businessImpact, priorityScore nullable, createdAt, updatedAt).

- Status enum: TODO, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, DONE
- Priority enum: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH

Repository — create, findById, findByGoal, findByAssignee, findByTeam, update, countByGoalAndStatus.

Service — TaskService.createTask(dto, caller): asserts the caller leads the team that owns the parent goal, validates estimatedHours > 0, defaults status to TODO. TaskService.updateTask for edits to title, description, priority, estimate and due date.

Controller — POST /goals/:goalId/tasks, GET /goals/:goalId/tasks, GET /tasks/:id, PATCH /tasks/:id.

Frontend

- Task list within Goal Details, showing status, priority, assignee, due date and estimate
- Task creation form: title, description, priority, estimated hours, due date
- Task detail view
- Visual priority indicator and an overdue marker
- Empty state when a goal has no tasks

Acceptance criteria

- A Team Lead can create a task under a goal belonging to their team
- Creating a task under another team's goal returns 403
- Estimated hours must be a positive number
- Tasks appear in the goal's task list immediately after creation
- A task can be created unassigned, and the UI shows that state clearly
- Task due date is validated against the parent goal's deadline — warn, don't block

Notes

Two fields are placed here but consumed in Epic 5: businessImpact and priorityScore. Both feed the recommendation formula. Adding them now is a deliberate choice to avoid a migration on a table that will already hold data by Day 3. priorityScore stays null until Epic 5 computes it.

estimatedHours is the hinge field of the whole application. It's entered here, compared against recorded time in Epic 3, drives the workload bands in Epic 4, and triggers the "actual exceeds estimate" risk in Epic 6. It deserves validation stricter than a plain number — reject zero and negatives at the Zod layer.

On task due dates past the goal deadline: warn rather than reject. Real teams have tasks that slip past a goal date, and that inconsistency is itself useful signal for the risk dashboard.

Dependencies

Depends on goal creation. Blocks task assignment, status updates, goal progress, all of Epic 3, and Epic 5.

issues.summary: Assign tasks to team members
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need to assign a task to a member of my team so that responsibility for the work is explicit.

Layer work

Entity — Task.assigneeId, already on the table. Create TaskAssignment only if the multiple-assignee decision below says so.

Repository — TaskRepository.updateAssignee(taskId, userId), TaskRepository.findByAssignee(userId, filter).

Service — TaskService.assignTask(taskId, assigneeId, caller):

- asserts the caller leads the team owning the task's goal
- asserts the assignee is a member of that same team — this is the rule that keeps work inside team boundaries
- allows reassignment and unassignment (null)

Controller — PUT /tasks/:id/assignee, Team Lead only.

Frontend

- Assignee dropdown on the task form and in the task list, populated only with members of the goal's team
- Reassignment from the task detail view
- Unassign action
- Assignee name and avatar initial shown on every task row

Acceptance criteria

- A Team Lead can assign a task to a member of their team
- Assigning to a user outside the team is rejected
- A Team Lead cannot assign tasks belonging to another team's goal
- A task can be reassigned, and can be returned to unassigned
- The assignee dropdown lists only eligible team members
- Employees cannot assign tasks, including to themselves

Decision — single or multiple assignees

The source doc leaves this open: "Create TaskAssignment model if multiple assignees are allowed."

Recommendation: a single assignee via Task.assigneeId. Reasons:

- The employee-facing story is "view my assigned tasks", which is unambiguous with one owner
- Epic 3 forbids logging time against unassigned tasks — with multiple assignees, "assigned to me" becomes a join rather than a column
- Epic 4's workload maths divides estimated hours per person; shared ownership needs a splitting rule the doc never specifies

If you want the realism of multiple assignees, add TaskAssignment now rather than later — retrofitting it after Epic 4 means rewriting every allocation query.

Dependencies

Depends on task creation and team membership. Blocks the employee task view, all of Epic 3, and Epic 4's per-person allocation.

issues.summary: Employee views assigned tasks and updates status
issues.description:
Story

As an Employee, I need one place that shows every task assigned to me and lets me update its status so that I know what to work on without chasing people in chat.

This is the story that solves the problem statement's complaint about employees receiving work through meetings and messages with no single home.

Layer work

Repository — TaskRepository.findByAssignee(userId, { status, dueBefore }) with the parent goal joined, so the UI can show which goal each task serves.

Service

- TaskService.getMyTasks(callerId, filter) — returns only tasks where assigneeId === callerId, never a broader set filtered client-side
- TaskService.updateStatus(taskId, status, caller) — an Employee may change status only on their own assigned tasks; a Team Lead may change status on any task in their team

Controller — GET /tasks/mine, PATCH /tasks/:id/status.

Frontend

- "My Tasks" page grouped or filterable by status
- Each row shows title, parent goal, deadline, priority, estimated hours, current status
- Inline status control moving a task between TODO, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, DONE
- Overdue tasks visually distinguished
- Sort by deadline and by priority
- Empty state for an employee with no assigned work

Acceptance criteria

- An Employee sees only tasks assigned to them
- An Employee changing the status of someone else's task receives 403
- Status changes persist and appear immediately in the goal's task list
- Each task displays its parent goal and deadline
- A Team Lead can change status on any task within their team
- The filtering happens server-side — the API must never return other people's tasks

Notes

The security point is worth stating plainly: GET /tasks/mine must filter in the repository query, not fetch the team's tasks and filter in React. The doc's acceptance criterion "employee sees only assigned tasks" is a data-access rule, not a display rule.

On the BLOCKED status. It is set manually here. Epic 5 introduces dependency-derived blocking, at which point there are two sources of truth for the same state. Decide then whether dependency-blocking overrides the manual flag or sits alongside it — flagging it now so it isn't a surprise on Day 3.

Dependencies

Depends on task assignment. Blocks Epic 3 — employees log time from this screen.

issues.summary: Goal progress calculation from completed tasks
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need each goal to show a progress percentage derived from its tasks so that I can see at a glance whether the goal is advancing toward its deadline.

Layer work

Repository — TaskRepository.countByGoalAndStatus(goalId) returning a status breakdown in a single grouped query, not one query per status.

Service — GoalService.calculateProgress(goalId):

progress = (tasks with status DONE / total tasks) * 100

Rules: a goal with zero tasks returns 0% and a "no tasks yet" flag rather than a divide-by-zero; the value is computed on read, never stored.

Controller — progress is included in the goal list and goal detail responses; no separate endpoint.

Frontend

- Progress bar on each goal card and on Goal Details
- Task status breakdown: total, done, in progress, blocked, to do
- Days remaining until deadline, with overdue shown distinctly
- "No tasks yet" state instead of a 0% bar on an empty goal

Acceptance criteria

- Goal progress equals completed tasks over total tasks, as a percentage
- A goal with no tasks shows an explanatory state, not 0%
- Progress updates immediately after any task status change
- Progress appears in both the goals list and goal details
- The calculation runs in one grouped database query per goal list, not N+1

Notes

Computed on read, not stored. A stored progressPercent column would need updating on every task status change, task creation, and task deletion — three write paths to keep in sync, and every one of them a chance to drift. At this data volume the calculation is trivial. If it ever becomes a bottleneck, cache it; don't denormalise it.

Simple count, not weighted by hours. Weighting progress by estimatedHours would arguably be more accurate — a goal with one 40-hour task and nine 1-hour tasks isn't 90% done when the small ones finish. But the source doc specifies "progress is calculated from completed tasks", and the honest count is easier to explain. Note the limitation rather than silently improving on the spec.

Watch the N+1. Listing ten goals must not fire ten count queries. This is the first place in the build where the repository layer earns its keep — one grouped query keyed by goalId.

Dependencies

Depends on task creation and status updates. Blocks Epic 4's goal-progress rollups and Epic 6's "goal progress below expectation" risk condition.

issues.summary: Employee logs daily time against an assigned task
issues.description:
Story

As an Employee, I need to record the hours I spent on an assigned task on a given date so that my team lead can see actual effort against the estimate.

Layer work

Entity — TimesheetEntry (id, employeeId FK, taskId FK, workDate date, hoursSpent decimal, workNote text, submissionStatus, createdAt, updatedAt). Index on (employeeId, workDate) — every later dashboard query filters on this pair.

Repository — create, findByEmployeeAndDate, findByEmployeeAndTaskAndDate, findByTask, sumHoursByTask, sumHoursByEmployeeInRange.

Service — TimesheetService.logTime(dto, caller) enforcing, in order:

1. the task exists and task.assigneeId === caller.userId — no logging against unassigned or other people's tasks
2. hoursSpent > 0 and hoursSpent <= MAX_DAILY_HOURS
3. the running daily total across all tasks stays within MAX_DAILY_HOURS
4. the duplicate rule below
5. workDate is not in the future

Controller — POST /timesheets, Employee only, Zod-validated.

Frontend

- "Log Time" action on each row of My Tasks
- Daily timesheet form: date picker defaulting to today, hours, work note
- Validation messages inline, per field
- Confirmation showing the new running total for that day

Two decisions to settle

1. Duplicate entries — reject or upsert? The doc offers both: "Prevent duplicate entries for the same task and date, or update the existing entry."

Recommendation: upsert. An employee logging two hours in the morning and three in the afternoon is normal behaviour, and a rejection there is user-hostile. Upsert adds to the existing entry for that (employee, task, date) and appends to the note. Whichever you choose, the frontend behaviour follows directly, so decide before writing the endpoint.

2. MAX_DAILY_HOURS. The doc says "validate maximum daily hours" without giving a number. Suggest 12 — high enough not to obstruct a genuinely long day, low enough to catch a typo like 80 instead of 8. Put it in config, not inline.

Acceptance criteria

- An Employee can log time only against a task assigned to them
- Logging against an unassigned or another employee's task returns 403
- Zero, negative, and non-numeric hours are rejected
- A single day's total across all tasks cannot exceed the configured maximum
- Future-dated entries are rejected
- The duplicate rule behaves as decided, consistently

Dependencies

Depends on task assignment and the employee task view. Blocks every other story in Epic 3, all of Epic 4, and Epic 6's estimate-overrun risk.

issues.summary: Employee edits and deletes their own time entries
issues.description:
Story

As an Employee, I need to correct or remove a time entry I logged earlier so that mistakes don't distort my team's effort figures.

Layer work

Repository — TimesheetRepository.update, TimesheetRepository.delete, TimesheetRepository.findById.

Service

- TimesheetService.updateEntry(entryId, dto, caller) — asserts entry.employeeId === caller.userId via assertOwnsResource; re-runs the same daily-total and hour-range validations as creation, so an edit cannot bypass rules that creation enforces
- TimesheetService.deleteEntry(entryId, caller) — same ownership assertion

Controller — PATCH /timesheets/:id, DELETE /timesheets/:id.

Frontend

- Edit and delete actions on each row of My Timesheet
- Edit form pre-filled with the current values
- Delete confirmation showing which task and date is being removed
- Optimistic update with rollback on failure

Acceptance criteria

- An Employee can edit hours and the work note on their own entry
- An Employee editing or deleting someone else's entry receives 403
- Edits are re-validated against the daily maximum — an edit cannot push the day over the limit
- A deleted entry disappears from task totals immediately
- A Team Lead cannot edit an employee's entry (they observe, they don't rewrite)

Notes

The validation-bypass trap. It's easy to put the hour rules only in logTime and let updateEntry write straight through. Then an employee logs 4 hours and edits it to 400. Both paths must call the same private validator — this is exactly the sort of duplication the service layer exists to prevent.

Why Team Leads can't edit. The doc gives leads view access to team timesheets and never grants edit. Keeping it that way preserves the entries as a record of what the employee actually claimed. If a correction is needed, the employee makes it.

On submissionStatus. The field exists on the entity but no approval workflow is in scope. Either leave it at a constant default or drop it from the API surface — an unused status field that appears in responses invites the assumption that approval exists.

Dependencies

Depends on time logging. Blocks nothing, but the timesheet history view is far less useful without it.

issues.summary: My Timesheet history with date filtering and totals
issues.description:
Story

As an Employee, I need to review the time I have logged over a chosen period so that I can check my own record before anyone else does.

Layer work

Repository — TimesheetRepository.findByEmployeeInRange(employeeId, from, to) with the task and parent goal joined, ordered by workDate descending. sumHoursByEmployeeGroupedByDate and sumHoursByEmployeeGroupedByTask as grouped queries.

Service — TimesheetService.getMyHistory(callerId, { from, to }):

- defaults to the current week when no range is supplied
- returns entries plus two rollups: totals by day and totals by task
- rejects a range where from is after to

Controller — GET /timesheets/mine?from=&to=.

Frontend

- My Timesheet page listing entries with date, task, goal, hours and note
- Date range filter with quick presets: this week, last week, this month
- Total hours per day, shown as a summary row or small bar chart
- Total hours per task across the selected range
- Empty state when no time is logged in the range

Acceptance criteria

- An Employee sees only their own entries, filtered server-side
- The date range filter narrows results correctly, inclusive of both endpoints
- Daily totals are correct and match the sum of the listed entries
- Per-task totals are correct across the range
- An invalid range (from after to) is rejected with a clear message
- The default view shows something useful without the user touching the filter

Notes

Default to the current week, not to everything. An unbounded query is fine with seed data and wrong in principle — the endpoint should never be able to return an employee's entire history by accident. Cap the maximum range as well.

Two rollups, not one list plus client-side maths. Summing in React works until the range grows, and it duplicates logic the dashboards in Epic 4 will need anyway. Do the grouping in SQL and return it.

Inclusive date boundaries. Off-by-one on to is the most likely bug in this story. Worth an explicit test: an entry dated exactly on the to boundary must appear.

Dependencies

Depends on time logging and entry editing. Shares its grouped-query helpers with Epic 4 — write them here with that reuse in mind.

issues.summary: Task effort totals and estimated-versus-actual comparison
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need to see the total time recorded against each task in my team and how it compares to the estimate so that I can tell where effort is going and where estimates were wrong.

Layer work

Repository — TimesheetRepository.sumHoursByTaskIds(taskIds) returning totals for a set of tasks in one grouped query.

Service

- TaskService.getTaskEffort(taskId, caller) — returns estimatedHours, actualHours, variance, variancePercent, and the contributing entries
- TimesheetService.getTeamTimesheets(teamId, { from, to }, caller) — asserts the caller leads that team; returns entries across all team members
- Variance classification lives here as a named function, because Epic 6's estimate-overrun risk must reuse it rather than reimplement the threshold

Controller — GET /tasks/:id/effort, GET /teams/:teamId/timesheets.

Frontend

- Estimated versus actual hours on the task detail view, with a variance indicator
- Progress-style bar showing consumed effort against estimate, visually distinct once it exceeds 100%
- Team timesheet view listing entries by member with a date filter
- Contributing entries visible from the task, so a total can be traced to its parts

Acceptance criteria

- Task detail shows total recorded time against the estimate
- A Team Lead can view timesheets for their own team only
- A Team Lead requesting another team's timesheets receives 403
- An Employee cannot view another employee's entries — this is an explicit criterion in the source doc
- Variance is correct, including the over-estimate case
- Tasks with no logged time show zero actual hours, not a broken or empty display

Notes

Define the overrun threshold now. "Actual hours exceed estimate" is an Epic 6 risk condition, and it needs a number: is 101% a risk, or 120%? Suggest a configurable threshold defaulting to 100% for display and something higher — say 120% — for raising a risk. Put the classifier in the service here so Epic 6 imports it.

The estimatedHours = 0 guard. Variance percent divides by the estimate. Task creation rejects zero estimates, but seed data and future imports may not, so guard the division rather than trusting the upstream validation.

Privacy boundary worth testing explicitly. "Employees cannot view other employees' timesheets" appears in the doc's acceptance criteria for both Epic 3 and Epic 4. It's the one rule in this epic a reviewer will actively try to break.

Dependencies

Depends on time logging and task creation. Blocks Epic 4's allocation table and Epic 6's overrun risk.

issues.summary: Workload calculation service and capacity classification
issues.description:
Story

As the system, I need a single service that computes each employee's workload against their capacity so that every dashboard and risk check reads the same number from the same place.

This is the calculation story. The two dashboard stories that follow are presentation over what this produces.

Layer work

Repository — AllocationRepository.getEmployeeWorkloadData(teamId, from, to): one query per team returning, per employee, the active task count, summed estimated hours on active tasks, summed recorded hours in range, completed count, and overdue count. This must not be N+1 — no looping over members firing a query each.

Service — AllocationService:

utilisation = (estimatedHoursOnActiveTasks / weeklyCapacityHours) * 100

0–60%   → Available
61–90%  → Balanced
>90%    → Overloaded

Exposed as classifyWorkload(estimatedHours, capacityHours), a pure function taking no repository — so it is unit-testable and importable by Epic 6.

Controller — none. This story ships no endpoint; it ships the calculation and its tests.

Definitions to pin down

- Active task — status TODO or IN_PROGRESS. Excludes DONE; include BLOCKED, because blocked work still occupies a person's plate
- Capacity — Team.weeklyCapacityHours, default 40
- Utilisation is based on estimated hours, not recorded hours. Recorded hours are the past; assigned estimates are the commitment. The doc's example table confirms this: Alex has 42 estimated against 30 recorded and is labelled Overloaded, which only works if the estimate drives the classification
- Range scaling — decide whether a two-week range doubles capacity or the bands apply per week. Weekly is simpler; document the choice

Acceptance criteria

- Utilisation is computed per employee from active-task estimates against team capacity
- The three bands classify correctly, including exactly at the 60% and 90% boundaries
- An employee with no active tasks returns 0% and Available, not an error
- The workload query for a team runs in constant query count regardless of member count
- classifyWorkload has unit tests covering each band and both boundaries
- The doc's worked example reproduces: Alex 5 tasks / 42 est / 30 rec → Overloaded; Priya 3 / 28 / 22 → Balanced; Sam 1 / 8 / 6 → Available

Notes

The boundaries are ambiguous in the source. "0–60 Available, 61–90 Balanced" leaves 60.5% unclassified. Treat the bands as ≤60, ≤90, >90 and state it in code.

Why a pure function matters here. Epic 6 needs "employee overloaded" as a risk. If that logic gets re-typed there against slightly different inputs, the dashboard and the risk panel will disagree with each other — and that kind of contradiction is very hard to debug from a screenshot.

Dependencies

Depends on task assignment, estimated hours, and time logging. Blocks both dashboard stories and Epic 6's overload risk.

issues.summary: Team Dashboard with KPIs and employee workload table
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need one dashboard showing my team's goals, task counts and per-employee workload so that I can answer "what is the team working on and who is overloaded" without opening five screens.

Layer work

Service — AllocationService.getTeamSummary(teamId, { from, to }, caller):

- asserts the caller leads the team (Super Admin passes through)
- returns team KPIs: active goals, total / completed / blocked / overdue task counts
- returns the per-employee allocation rows from the workload service
- returns goal progress for each active goal

Controller — GET /teams/:teamId/summary?from=&to=.

Frontend

- Team Dashboard as the Team Lead's landing page
- KPI cards: active goals, total tasks, completed, blocked, overdue
- Employee workload table — the doc's shape:

Employee

Active tasks

Estimated hours

Recorded hours

Workload

Alex

5

42

30

Overloaded

Priya

3

28

22

Balanced

Sam

1

8

6

Available

- Colour-coded workload badges
- Active goals list with progress bars
- Loading skeletons and an empty state for a team with no goals

Acceptance criteria

- A Team Lead sees the dashboard for their own team only
- Requesting another team's summary returns 403
- The workload column matches the classification service exactly
- Overdue counts only tasks past dueDate and not DONE
- Date-range filtering changes recorded hours but not the active-task estimate
- An employee with no tasks still appears in the table, showing zero

Notes

One endpoint, not five. It's tempting to have the dashboard call /goals, /tasks, /timesheets and stitch results in React. Don't — the aggregation belongs server-side, and a single summary endpoint is also what makes the Super Admin view in the next story a small change rather than a rewrite.

Employees with zero tasks must not vanish. An inner join on tasks silently drops them, which is precisely backwards: an idle person is the most actionable row in a resource dashboard. Left join from members.

"Overdue" needs one definition, used everywhere. Past due date and not DONE. Epic 6 raises overdue as a risk; same definition, same helper.

Dependencies

Depends on the workload calculation service and goal progress. Blocks the company-wide overview, which generalises this endpoint.

issues.summary: Super Admin company-wide allocation overview with filters
issues.description:
Story

As a Super Admin, I need a company-wide view across all teams so that I can compare team health and spot where resources are misallocated at the organisation level.

Layer work

Repository — AllocationRepository.getCompanyWorkloadData(from, to): the same shape as the team query but unscoped, grouped by team. One query, not one per team.

Service — AllocationService.getCompanySummary({ from, to, teamId, goalId }, caller):

- Super Admin only
- returns company totals plus a per-team breakdown: member count, active goals, task counts, average utilisation, overloaded and available member counts
- accepts optional filters that narrow to a team, a goal, or a date range

Controller — GET /company/summary?from=&to=&teamId=&goalId=.

Frontend

- Super Admin company overview as their landing page
- Company KPI cards: total teams, total employees, active goals, total tasks, overdue count
- Per-team comparison table with average utilisation and an overloaded-member count
- Drill-through from a team row into that team's dashboard
- Filter bar: team, employee, date range
- Company-wide employee allocation table, filterable

Acceptance criteria

- Super Admin sees every team; Team Leads and Employees receive 403
- Company totals equal the sum of the per-team figures
- Filters compose — team plus date range applies both
- Clicking a team opens that team's dashboard
- The overloaded/available counts use the same classification as the team view
- The response is produced in constant query count regardless of team count

Notes

This is a filter change, not a new dashboard. If the team summary was built as a scoped query rather than a hardcoded one, this story is mostly removing the scope and grouping one level higher. If it turns out to need substantially new code, the team endpoint was built too narrowly — worth fixing there rather than duplicating here.

Average utilisation across a team is a weak statistic and worth presenting carefully. A team with one person at 150% and three at 20% averages to a healthy-looking 52%. Show the overloaded count alongside the average, or the dashboard will hide precisely the problem it exists to reveal.

Filter composition is where this breaks. Team plus date plus goal must AND together. Build the query with a composable where-clause rather than branching on which filters are present.

Dependencies

Depends on the team dashboard and the workload service. Blocks Epic 6's company-wide risk overview, which reuses the same scoping pattern.

issues.summary: Task dependencies with self-reference and cycle detection
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need to declare that one task depends on another so that the system knows what cannot start yet and what is holding up other work.

This is the most algorithmically interesting story in the build — the dependency graph and its cycle check.

Layer work

Entity — TaskDependency (id, taskId, dependsOnTaskId, createdAt) with a unique constraint on (taskId, dependsOnTaskId). Read as: taskId is blocked by dependsOnTaskId.

Repository — create, delete, findDependenciesOf(taskId), findDependentsOf(taskId), findAllEdgesForGoal(goalId).

Service — DependencyService.addDependency(taskId, dependsOnTaskId, caller), validating in order:

1. caller leads the team owning both tasks
2. taskId !== dependsOnTaskId — reject direct self-dependency
3. both tasks exist and belong to the same team
4. the edge doesn't already exist
5. no cycle is created — see below

Cycle detection

Before inserting the edge A → B, check whether B can already reach A by following existing edges. If it can, the new edge closes a loop; reject it.

- Depth-first traversal over findDependenciesOf, with a visited set
- Load the goal's edges once and traverse in memory rather than querying per hop
- Cap the depth as a safety net against unexpected data
- Return a message naming the tasks in the cycle, not a bare "invalid dependency"

Controller — POST /tasks/:id/dependencies, DELETE /tasks/:id/dependencies/:dependsOnId, GET /tasks/:id/dependencies.

Frontend

- Dependency selector on the task form, listing only tasks within the same goal or team
- Task detail showing two lists: "blocked by" and "blocks"
- Remove-dependency action
- Cycle rejection surfaced as a readable explanation of which tasks form the loop

Acceptance criteria

- A task can depend on one or more other tasks
- A task depending on itself is rejected
- A dependency creating a cycle (A→B→C→A) is rejected, and the message names the cycle
- Duplicate edges are rejected
- Both directions are visible from the task detail
- A dependency spanning two different teams is rejected
- The seed data includes a deliberate circular case for testing, per the source doc

Notes

Direction is the thing people get wrong. Pick one reading, put it in a comment above the entity, and never restate it differently elsewhere. Here: a row means "taskId waits for dependsOnTaskId".

Cycle detection must run before the write, inside the same transaction. Insert-then-check leaves a window where a cycle exists in the database.

Dependencies

Depends on task creation. Blocks blocked-state calculation and priority scoring — dependency impact is a scoring input.

issues.summary: Blocked-state calculation from unfinished prerequisites
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need the system to work out which tasks are actually blocked by unfinished prerequisites so that nobody picks up work that cannot be started.

Layer work

Service — DependencyService.computeBlockedState(taskId):

A task is blocked when at least one task it depends on has status != DONE.

Returns the blocked flag plus the list of blocking tasks, since the UI and the recommendation explanations both need the reason, not just the boolean.

DependencyService.computeBlockedStates(taskIds) — the batch version. Dashboards and the recommendation endpoint need this for a whole goal at once, so build it as the primary method and let the single-task version delegate to it.

DependencyService.countDependents(taskId) — how many tasks this one is blocking. Feeds the "+10 per blocked task" scoring term.

Controller — no new endpoint. Blocked state is included in task responses.

The decision this story forces

BLOCKED already exists as a manual status from Epic 2. Now there are two sources of truth for the same idea. Three options:

1. Derived overrides manual — dependency blocking wins; manual BLOCKED becomes meaningless
2. Manual wins — derived state is ignored when a human has set the status
3. Separate concepts — status stays human-controlled; add a computed isBlocked alongside it, and treat a task as unavailable if either is true

Recommendation: option 3. They genuinely are different things — "waiting on TASK-104" and "blocked because the vendor hasn't replied" are both real, and collapsing them loses information. It also avoids a background job rewriting statuses humans set.

Whichever you pick, the -40 blocked penalty in the scoring formula must apply to the same definition the UI displays.

Acceptance criteria

- A task with an unfinished prerequisite is reported as blocked
- A task whose prerequisites are all DONE is not blocked
- A task with no dependencies is never blocked by this rule
- Completing the last prerequisite clears the derived blocked state immediately
- The blocking reason lists the specific tasks responsible
- Batch computation for a goal runs in constant query count
- Manual and derived blocking interact as decided, and the rule is documented

Notes

Only direct prerequisites count. If A waits on B and B waits on C, A is blocked by B regardless of C. Transitive blocking is real but adds nothing here — B already reports its own reason, and the chain is visible by following it.

Dependencies

Depends on task dependencies. Blocks priority scoring and Epic 6's "high-priority task blocked" risk.

issues.summary: Priority score calculation service
issues.description:
Story

As the system, I need to compute a priority score for each task from its business priority, deadline, dependency impact and blocked state so that work can be ranked objectively.

The formula

Priority score =
  Business priority
+ Deadline urgency
+ Dependency impact
+ Goal importance
- Blocked penalty

High priority:       +30      Due within 2 days:   +30
Medium priority:     +20      Due within 7 days:   +20
Low priority:        +10      Due later:            +5

Blocks another task: +10 per task
Currently blocked:   -40

Layer work

Service — PriorityService.calculateScore(task, context), a pure function taking the task, its dependent count, its blocked state and its goal importance. No repository access, no database, fully unit-testable.

PriorityService.scoreTasksForTeam(teamId) — the batch orchestrator: loads tasks, dependent counts and blocked states in bulk, then maps the pure scorer over them.

Each score is returned with its component breakdown, not just a total. The explanation story downstream needs to say "+30 high priority, +30 due tomorrow, +20 blocks two tasks" — and reconstructing that from a single number afterwards is impossible.

Controller — no endpoint of its own; scores appear on task responses and drive the recommendation endpoint.

Values the doc leaves undefined

- Goal importance — not given a scale. Suggest mirroring task priority: High +20, Medium +10, Low +5
- Estimated effort — listed as a signal but absent from the formula. Leave it out. Adding an undocumented term makes the score unexplainable, which defeats the purpose
- No due date — treat as "due later" (+5)
- Overdue — the doc stops at "within 2 days". Suggest overdue scores at least as high as +30; an overdue task is not less urgent than a task due tomorrow

Recalculation

The doc requires recalculation when deadlines, status or dependencies change. Compute on read. The inputs change constantly and a stored score would need invalidating from four different write paths. Persist to Task.priorityScore only if read performance genuinely demands it.

Acceptance criteria

- The score matches the published formula for every documented combination
- calculateScore is pure, with unit tests for each term and the boundaries (exactly 2 days, exactly 7 days)
- A blocked task receives the full −40 penalty
- Dependency impact scales with the number of dependents
- Every score carries a component breakdown
- Batch scoring for a team runs in constant query count
- Scores update when a deadline, status or dependency changes

Notes

Weights are constants in config, not literals scattered through the code. They will be tuned once someone looks at the output and disagrees with it.

Dependencies

Depends on blocked-state calculation, dependency counts, and goal importance. Blocks the recommendation endpoint.

issues.summary: Recommended tasks endpoint with ranked results and explanations
issues.description:
Story

As a Team Lead, I need a ranked list of recommended next tasks with an explanation for each so that the team works on the right thing and I can see why the system thinks so.

An unexplained ranking is one nobody trusts. The explanation is the feature, not decoration on it.

Layer work

Service — PriorityService.getRecommendations(teamId, { assigneeId, limit }, caller):

- asserts the caller leads the team
- excludes DONE tasks and, by default, blocked ones — blocked work isn't actionable, so the −40 penalty demotes rather than surfaces it
- sorts by score descending, ties broken by nearest deadline
- builds a human-readable reason list from the score breakdown

Explanation builder — turns score components into sentences:

Recommended next task: TASK-108

Reasons:
- High business priority
- Due tomorrow
- Blocks three other tasks
- Assigned employee is available
- All prerequisites are complete

Two reasons come from outside the score: assignee availability (from Epic 4's workload classification) and prerequisite completion (from the blocked-state service). Both are pulled in here rather than folded into the number.

Controller — GET /teams/:teamId/recommendations?assigneeId=&limit=.

Frontend

- Recommended Tasks section on the Team Dashboard
- Each card: title, score, assignee, deadline, and the reason list
- Score breakdown on hover or expand, showing each term's contribution
- Sort-by-priority option on the main task list
- High-impact tasks (blocking several others) visually marked
- Optional per-employee filter: "what should Priya do next?"

Acceptance criteria

- Recommendations are ranked by descending priority score
- Every recommendation carries at least one concrete reason
- Blocked tasks do not appear in the default recommendations
- DONE tasks never appear
- Filtering by assignee returns only that person's actionable tasks
- The reasons shown reconcile with the score breakdown — no reason without a corresponding term
- An empty state appears when every task is blocked or complete

Notes

Reasons must be generated from the score components, not written separately. If the explanation is assembled by a second pass of independent logic, it will eventually contradict the number beside it — and a recommendation that contradicts its own reasoning is worse than no recommendation.

"Assigned employee is available" needs a rule for unassigned tasks. An unassigned task has no availability to check. Either omit that reason or surface "unassigned" as its own signal — arguably a positive one, since anyone could pick it up.

Dependencies

Depends on priority scoring, blocked state, and the Epic 4 workload classification. Final story of Epic 5.

issues.summary: Project risk calculation service covering eight risk conditions
issues.description:
Story

As a manager, I need the system to detect delivery risks across my team so that I can act before a deadline is missed rather than explain afterwards why it was.

This is the must-ship story of Phase 3. If Day 3 compresses, everything else in Epic 6 goes before this does.

The eight conditions

Condition

Rule

Severity

Task overdue

past dueDate, not DONE

High if high-priority, else Medium

High-priority task blocked

blocked and priority HIGH

High

Goal deadline approaching

within N days of deadline, not complete

Medium

Goal progress below expectation

progress % lags elapsed-time % by a margin

Medium/High by gap

Unassigned task

no assignee, goal is ACTIVE

Medium

Employee overloaded

utilisation above 90%

Medium

Actual hours exceed estimate

over the configured overrun threshold

Medium

No recent progress

no status change or time logged in N days

Low/Medium

Layer work

Service — RiskService, one detector per condition, each a small function returning zero or more risk objects (type, severity, entityId, entityType, message, detectedAt). RiskService.detectTeamRisks(teamId) runs all eight and returns a sorted list.

Critically: each detector imports the existing helper rather than reimplementing the rule.

- overdue → the shared overdue definition from Epic 4
- blocked → DependencyService.computeBlockedStates
- overloaded → AllocationService.classifyWorkload
- overrun → the variance classifier from Epic 3
- goal progress → GoalService.calculateProgress

Controller — GET /teams/:teamId/risks, GET /company/risks (Super Admin).

Thresholds the doc leaves open

- Deadline approaching: suggest 3 days
- Progress below expectation: compare progress % against elapsed % of the start-to-deadline window; flag when it lags by more than 20 points
- No recent progress: suggest 5 days since the last status change or timesheet entry
- All configurable, none inline

Acceptance criteria

- All eight conditions are detected against seeded data
- Each risk carries a type, severity, message and a link to the entity
- Risks are computed on demand, not stored
- Detection for a team runs in a bounded number of queries — no per-task loops
- A Team Lead sees only their team's risks; a Super Admin sees all
- Each detector has unit tests, including the boundary case
- The same task appearing under two conditions produces two distinct risks, not one merged entry

Notes

No duplicated rules. If "overdue" is written a second time here with a subtly different comparison, the dashboard and the risk panel will disagree — and a manager who spots that stops trusting both.

Compute on read. Risks are derived state over data that changes constantly. Persisting them means invalidation from a dozen write paths.

Dependencies

Depends on Epics 2, 3, 4 and 5. Blocks the risk overview UI.

issues.summary: Risk Overview UI with severity grouping and drill-through
issues.description:
Story

As a manager, I need all detected risks in one place, grouped by severity, so that I can see what needs attention without reading every task.

Frontend

- Risk Overview section on both the Team Dashboard and the company overview
- Severity grouping: High, Medium, Low — with counts
- Card types matching the doc's list:
  - Overdue task cards — title, assignee, days overdue
  - Blocked task cards — title, priority, what is blocking it
  - Overloaded resource warnings — employee, utilisation %, active task count
  - Goal-at-risk cards — goal, progress vs elapsed time, days to deadline
- Every card links through to the underlying task, goal, or employee
- Filter by severity and by risk type
- "No risks detected" as a deliberate, reassuring state rather than an empty box
- Simple charts: goal progress, and resource allocation across the team

Layer work

No new backend logic. This story consumes GET /teams/:teamId/risks and GET /company/risks.

Acceptance criteria

- Risks are grouped and sorted by severity, highest first
- Each card explains the risk in a sentence a manager can act on
- Every card navigates to the entity it describes
- A Team Lead sees only their team's risks; a Super Admin sees all, grouped by team
- Filtering by severity and type works together
- The empty state is explicit
- Loading and error states are handled — a failed risk fetch must not blank the whole dashboard

Notes

Severity ordering is the whole point of the screen. A manager should be able to read the top three cards and stop. If everything renders as one flat list, the feature has failed even though the data is correct.

Messages should name the thing and the number. "TASK-108 is 4 days overdue and assigned to Alex" beats "Overdue task detected." The risk service already carries the values; use them.

Charts are the first thing to cut. They're listed in the doc under the same epic as the risk cards, but the cards carry the information and the charts decorate it. If Day 3 runs short, ship the cards.

Dependencies

Depends on the risk calculation service and both dashboards. Nothing depends on this.

issues.summary: Activity logging and recent-activity timeline
issues.description:
Story

As a manager, I need a record of significant changes so that I can see what happened, when, and who did it — without asking around.

Layer work

Entity — ActivityLog (id, actorId, entityType, entityId, action, oldValue, newValue, teamId, createdAt). Index on (teamId, createdAt) and (entityType, entityId).

Repository — create, findByTeam(teamId, { limit, before }), findByEntity(entityType, entityId).

Service — ActivityService.log(entry), called from the services that own each change:

- task status changed — TaskService.updateStatus
- task assigned or reassigned — TaskService.assignTask
- task priority changed — TaskService.updateTask
- timesheet created, updated, deleted — TimesheetService
- goal created and status changed — GoalService
- dependency added or removed — DependencyService

ActivityService.getRecentActivity(teamId, { limit }, caller) — scoped to the caller's team, Super Admin sees all.

Controller — GET /teams/:teamId/activity, GET /company/activity.

Frontend

- Recent-activity timeline on the Team Dashboard
- Each entry: actor, action, entity, timestamp, and the before/after where it applies
- Grouped by day, most recent first
- Per-entity history on task detail: "this task's changes"
- Load-more pagination
- Empty state for a quiet team

Acceptance criteria

- All listed change types produce a log entry
- Each entry records actor, entity, action, timestamp, and old/new values where meaningful
- A Team Lead sees only their team's activity
- Logging failure never fails the originating operation
- The timeline paginates rather than loading everything
- Task detail shows that task's own history

Notes

Log from the service, not from middleware or a database trigger. Only the service knows the domain meaning of the change — that status: TODO → IN_PROGRESS is "started work" rather than a column update.

Logging must not be able to break the write it describes. Wrap the log call so a failure is swallowed and reported, not propagated. An audit trail that can roll back a legitimate task update is worse than no audit trail.

This story matters to the context engine. Activity logs are the closest thing TrackIt produces to a change history with human intent attached — actor, entity, before, after. That is exactly the kind of artifact Context Core needs for "has a similar change been made before?" So record the domain action, not just the field diff, and keep entity references stable and resolvable.

Dependencies

Depends on all the services it hooks into. Blocks the recent-activity timeline only. First candidate for cutting if Day 3 compresses — behind search, ahead of nothing.

issues.summary: Global task search, filtering, and in-app notifications
issues.description:
Story

As any user, I need to find a specific task quickly and be told when something needs my attention so that I don't have to browse goal by goal.

Two smaller capabilities combined because neither justifies its own story and both are late-stage polish.

Search and filtering

Repository — TaskRepository.search({ query, teamId, status, assigneeId, priority, dueBefore, dueAfter }) with a composable where-clause, case-insensitive ILIKE on title and description, and pagination.

Service — TaskService.search(filters, caller). The caller's scope is applied before the filters, never after: an Employee searches only their own tasks, a Team Lead only their team's, Super Admin everything.

Controller — GET /tasks/search?q=&status=&assigneeId=&priority=&teamId=&dueBefore=.

Notifications

Entity — Notification (id, userId, type, message, entityType, entityId, isRead, createdAt).

Service — NotificationService.notify(userId, type, message, entity), triggered on: task assigned to you, your task's deadline is near, your task became blocked, your task went overdue. Plus markAsRead and getUnread.

Controller — GET /notifications, PATCH /notifications/:id/read, POST /notifications/read-all.

Frontend

- Global search in the header, with results grouped by team or goal
- Filter bar: team, status, assignee, deadline, priority — composable
- Notification bell with unread count
- Notification dropdown; clicking navigates to the entity and marks as read
- "Mark all read"
